That looks great! My wife does a lot of tanning and I help her now and then as a laborer, as it is somewhat labor intensive. While there are a mind boggling array of processes, the main ingredient in all of them seems to be plenty of elbow grease. She mainly does brain tan for buckskin. She uses a similar frame to stretch the hide for working it. She has taken to using an old wringer washing machine to work the brain solution into the hides. This cuts down on the physical labor quite a bit. If you brain tan and then smoke the hide, you will have buckskin that can get wet and then dry out again without stiffening up, which unsmoked buckskin will. That is important for garment leather, not so much so for harness, sheath, and scabbard type uses. She has also used bark. We don't have oak, but have plenty of hemlock, which is similarly high in tannin. She did a moose hide in hemlock bark that turned out very nicely. It was simpler than brain tanning in that she just boiled up a bunch of finely ground bark, resulting in a liquor similar in appearance to coffee. The hide was submerged in this until the liquor was clear, then the same bark was boiled up again and the whole thing repeated. It seems like she did that three or four times over several months. The finished hide wound up dyed a beautiful reddish brown color. She was going to cut it up and make something out of it, so she overtanned it with chrome, as that also makes a leather that can get wet and dry out without stiffening. (The biggest single recommendation for the chrome tan process.) In the end, it was too pretty to cut up, so we draped it over a chair and it has been there ever since! Her latest project was a rattlesnake hide we picked up in our travels. That was done with glycerin and alcohol. It turned out nice and soft, and we have high hopes for trying that method on fish skins as well now. Good luck on your project and your salted hides awaiting. The greatest thing you can do for a harvested animal is use every possible part of it for something!
